questions.stem: A client receiving continuous gastric tube feeding has slid down in bed so the head of the bed is elevated only 10 degrees. There is no medical contraindication to elevation. Which nursing action best reduces aspiration risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Pause the feeding only during sleep and keep the client nearly supine, because continuous enteral nutrition is safest when abdominal pressure is minimized.","B":"Reposition the client and maintain head-of-bed elevation at about 30 to 45 degrees, while continuing the other prescribed aspiration-prevention measures.","C":"Keep the head of the bed at 10 degrees and increase the feeding rate, because a shorter feeding duration reduces exposure to aspiration risk.","D":"Turn the client fully onto one side with the head of the bed flat, because lateral positioning provides the same aspiration protection as elevation."}}
questions.rationale: For adults receiving tube feeding, aspiration-prevention practice includes maintaining head-of-bed elevation at 30 to 45 degrees unless contraindicated, along with ongoing feeding-tube and gastrointestinal tolerance assessment. Keeping the client nearly supine or simply changing feeding speed does not provide equivalent protection.
questions.source_name: AACN — Prevention of Aspiration in Adults
questions.source_detail: AACN expected practice includes maintaining head-of-bed elevation at 30–45 degrees unless contraindicated for patients at aspiration risk, including tube-fed adults.

questions.stem: An infant is due for several routine vaccines at the same well-child visit. The parent asks whether receiving more than one vaccine today will overwhelm the infant’s immune system. Which response is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"“The vaccines should be separated by several weeks because simultaneous vaccination increases immune-system overload in otherwise healthy infants.”","B":"“Give no more than two injections in one limb today and defer any additional recommended vaccines, because extra antigens should be separated for safety.”","C":"“Recommended vaccines can be given during the same visit at appropriate separate sites; receiving multiple vaccines at once has been shown to be safe.”","D":"“The vaccines may be combined into one syringe to reduce the number of injections, even when the products are not manufactured as a combination vaccine.”"}}
questions.rationale: CDC states that receiving multiple recommended vaccines at the same visit has been shown to be safe. Coadministered injectable vaccines should be prepared separately and given at appropriate injection sites; clinicians should not create their own combination vaccine by mixing products in one syringe unless the product is manufactured and indicated as a combination vaccine.
questions.source_name: CDC — Multiple Vaccines at Once and Vaccine Administration
questions.source_detail: CDC: multiple vaccines at the same visit are safe; use separate syringes/sites as appropriate and do not mix vaccine products into an improvised combination.

questions.stem: During a preventive visit, a 16-year-old asks to speak with the health care professional without a parent present about sexual health concerns. Which nursing response is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"“Private time is appropriate only for services a minor can consent to independently; routine preventive counseling requires a parent to remain present for the discussion.”","B":"“Private time is developmentally appropriate; we will explain confidentiality and its limits and follow the laws and policies that apply where care is provided.”","C":"“We can speak privately, and the details will remain confidential unless a safety concern or applicable legal requirement permits or requires disclosure.”","D":"“Private discussion can occur only after your parent authorizes it, because parental permission determines confidentiality during a minor’s preventive visit.”"}}
questions.rationale: AAP considers confidential care an essential component of high-quality adolescent care and recommends consistent opportunities for time alone with adolescents as developmentally appropriate. Confidentiality is not absolute: clinicians must explain its limits and follow applicable federal/state law and practice requirements, including circumstances involving safety or mandated disclosure.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Confidentiality in the Care of Adolescents: Policy Statement
questions.source_detail: AAP 2024 recommends developmentally appropriate private time, respect for confidentiality when legally permitted or required, explanation of limits, and awareness of jurisdiction-specific law.

questions.stem: A client who may become pregnant within the next several months asks when to begin folic acid to reduce the risk of neural tube defects. Which recommendation is most appropriate for an average-risk client?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Begin folic acid only after pregnancy is confirmed by a missed period, because neural tube development does not begin until later in the first trimester.","B":"Wait until the second trimester to begin supplementation, because folic acid has no preventive role during the weeks around conception.","C":"Rely on naturally occurring food folate alone before pregnancy, then begin a supplement only if prenatal testing identifies a fetal abnormality.","D":"Take 400 mcg of folic acid daily before conception and during early pregnancy, because neural tube formation and closure occur very early."}}
questions.rationale: For an average-risk person who could become pregnant, CDC recommends 400 mcg of folic acid daily. Neural tube formation and closure occur very early in pregnancy, often before pregnancy is recognized, so supplementation should begin before conception and continue during early pregnancy rather than waiting for a positive test or a later trimester.
questions.source_name: CDC — Folic Acid: Sources and Recommended Intake / Neural Tube Defects
questions.source_detail: CDC 2026 recommends 400 mcg folic acid daily for people capable of becoming pregnant; CDC notes neural tube defects develop very early and folic acid before and during early pregnancy helps prevent them.

questions.stem: A client who has just learned that cancer treatment will be more extensive than expected says, “I don’t know how I’m going to handle this.” Which response best demonstrates therapeutic communication?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"“It sounds overwhelming. Tell me more about what feels hardest to manage right now, and we can work through your concerns together.”","B":"“Try to stay positive and focus on the treatment plan, because worrying about what might happen can make coping more difficult.”","C":"“Many people adjust once treatment starts, so give yourself a few days before deciding that the situation feels too difficult to manage.”","D":"“Let me explain the entire treatment schedule now so you can concentrate on the medical facts instead of the emotions you are experiencing.”"}}
questions.rationale: The response names and explores the client's emotion instead of minimizing it, giving unsolicited advice, or overwhelming the client with information. NCI's communication guidance describes empathic responses such as the NURSE framework, including naming, understanding, supporting, and exploring emotion with prompts such as asking the patient to say more about how they feel.
questions.source_name: National Cancer Institute — Communication in Cancer Care (PDQ), Health Professional Version
questions.source_detail: NCI communication guidance supports empathic exploration of emotion through strategies such as NURSE and Ask-Tell-Ask rather than false reassurance or information overload.

questions.stem: A bereaved client alternates between disbelief, intense sadness, periods of normal activity, and renewed grief when reminded of the loss. Which nursing interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Grief can fluctuate rather than follow a fixed sequence; the nurse should assess coping, function, safety, supports, and the client’s individual response over time.","B":"The client is grieving incorrectly because denial must resolve completely before sadness occurs and normal activity should not return until acceptance develops.","C":"The return of grief after a period of normal activity establishes prolonged grief disorder, so the nurse should classify the response as pathologic immediately.","D":"The recurring sadness shows the client has moved backward in the grief process, so care should focus on returning the client to the prior stage before normal activity can resume."}}
questions.rationale: Contemporary bereavement evidence does not support forcing grief into a fixed linear sequence. NCI notes that people may move back and forth among grief domains and that grief is highly individual. The nurse should assess function, coping, safety, supports, cultural context, and persistence/severity of symptoms rather than labeling normal fluctuation as failure to progress through a stage model.
questions.source_name: National Cancer Institute — Grief, Bereavement, and Coping With Loss (PDQ), Health Professional Version
questions.source_detail: NCI notes there is no preestablished linear grief process; the five-stage model has limited empirical support and grief domains can wax and wane without a fixed progression.

questions.stem: A highly agitated client in a day room is pacing, shouting, and gripping a chair while several other clients are nearby. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Approach within arm’s reach while another nurse observes and begin assessing the trigger, because close therapeutic presence can reduce escalating agitation safely.","B":"Administer a PRN sedative before changing the environment, because medication should precede other de-escalation measures when an object is being held.","C":"Leave the client in the day room but move staff farther away and wait for spontaneous calming, because additional interaction may intensify agitation before assessment.","D":"Increase distance, clear nearby people from immediate danger, call for support, and use a calm de-escalation approach while maintaining a safe exit route."}}
questions.rationale: When a person is escalating while holding an object that could be used as a weapon, immediate scene safety precedes detailed exploration. The nurse should create distance, move bystanders out of danger, summon assistance, preserve an exit route, and use calm de-escalation. Approaching within striking distance, waiting in a crowded environment, or treating medication as the automatic first intervention can increase risk.
questions.source_name: SAMHSA — Creating Safe Scenes / National Behavioral Health Crisis Care Guidance
questions.source_detail: SAMHSA crisis resources emphasize safety for both responders and people in crisis and use of safe, positive de-escalation approaches with timely support.
